planting.note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm soil, since this thin-walled pepper stalls badly in cool snaps.

directions: Carliston is a long, slightly curved, light-green frying pepper from western Turkey that ripens to red if left on the plant, though most cooks pick it green for quick pan-frying in olive oil. Stake plants in windy sites since the long pods make branches top-heavy, and pick continuously to keep production going through the season. It is a staple of Turkish meze tables, served blistered whole with salt and a squeeze of lemon.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil has warmed well past last frost, giving vines a long hot season to fully sweeten.

directions: Named for the town of Kırkağaç in Manisa province, this Aegean landrace melon has smooth pale-green to cream rind and firm, sweet white flesh that keeps for weeks after harvest, which historically made it a favored melon for winter storage and market transport. Pinch vines to encourage branching and reduce watering as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Unripe fruits are also eaten as a crisp salad vegetable in the same tradition as Turkish 'kelek'.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring on a semi-dwarf rootstock and stake until well established.

directions: Amasya is an old Ottoman-era apple traditionally grown along the Yeşilırmak valley in the Turkish city of the same name, prized for its aromatic, crisp, red-striped fruit and long storage life. Prune to an open center to admit light and air, which keeps fruit cleaner and sweeter in the humid river-valley climate it originates from. Beyond fresh eating, Amasya apples are famously threaded and air-dried into decorative dried-apple garlands, a regional specialty sold in the city's markets.
sources: Turkish Ministry of Agriculture pomology registry

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and trellis vines to keep the short fruit straight and clean for pickling.

directions: This small, thin-skinned, blocky cucumber takes its name from the Çengelköy neighborhood on the Bosphorus shore of Istanbul, where it was once grown in riverside market gardens and sold by street vendors still attached to the vine. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest young and small, since the variety is prized for crunch rather than size and turns seedy quickly if left too long. It is traditionally eaten fresh with coarse salt as a snack or lightly pickled.
sources: Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality heritage seed program

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in a frost-protected site, since early bloom makes flower buds vulnerable to late cold.

directions: Hacıhaliloğlu is the leading cultivar behind Turkey's famous Malatya dried-apricot trade, grown in orchards along the upper Euphrates where hot, dry summers are ideal for sun-drying the orange, richly flavored fruit. Choose a sheltered, south-facing slope to reduce frost damage to early blossoms, and thin fruit to improve size and sugar content. The fruit is eaten fresh, dried whole for export, or stuffed with nuts as a traditional Turkish confection.

planting.note: Plant bare-root in fall or early spring in well-drained soil; quince tolerates damper ground better than most tree fruit.

directions: Eşme quince takes its name from a district of Uşak province in the Aegean region of Turkey, long known for producing unusually large, intensely fragrant fruit prized above smaller wild quince types. Prune lightly to an open bowl shape, since quince fruits on short spurs and heavy pruning reduces yield. The fruit is inedible raw but turns rosy and aromatic when cooked, and in Turkey it is the classic base for ayva tatlısı, a syrup-poached quince dessert served with clotted cream.
sources: Turkish Ministry of Agriculture pomology registry
